title: Planting Seeds
strapline: Soil, a pot and a seed that is yours to water — and the long wait until something green appears.
intent: Children understand how plants grow and change over time by growing one themselves.
A plant that depends on their watering is a real, daily responsibility.
Waiting days for a shoot builds patience in a way nothing quick can.
Children observe and describe change over time, which is the heart of scientific noticing.
Handling soil, seeds and water is a rich sensory experience in its own right.
implementation: Provide soil, pots and easy-to-grow seeds — cress, beans and sunflowers all reward quickly enough.
Let each child plant and label their own pot so ownership is unambiguous.
Model planting: a hole this deep, one seed, cover it, water it — then let them do it.
Establish a watering routine the children run, not the adults.
Talk about what a seed needs — soil, water, light, warmth — and test what happens without one.
Encourage children to describe what they see as the plant sprouts, day by day.
Keep a growth record: a drawing or a photo each week beside the pots.
key_questions: What do you think your seed needs to grow?
How tall do you think it will be by next week?
What would happen if we forgot to water it?
Which pot has grown the most? Why do you think that is?

impact.text: Children plant, tend and care for a living thing as a real responsibility.
Children observe and describe change over time.
Children develop responsibility and keep to a routine that matters.
Children compare heights and amounts — taller, shorter, more, less.
Children keep going with a slow task over many days.
Children ask real questions and make predictions about what will happen.

enhancements: A clear jar with a bean against the glass so roots as well as shoots can be watched.
A control pot deliberately left unwatered or in the dark, to compare.
A measuring strip beside the pots so growth can be tracked in cubes or hand-spans.
A growing patch outdoors for the seedlings to be planted out into.
A harvest and taste when the cress is ready — growing something you then eat.
A photo diary each child takes home with their plant at the end of term.

playing_exploring: Children handle soil, seeds and water freely as materials in their own right.
Planting is hands-in, open and satisfying before anything even grows.
active_learning: Children tend their plant daily over weeks without losing interest.
The slow reward builds genuine persistence.
creating_thinking: Children predict what a seed needs and test it against a control.
They reason about why one pot has done better than another.
